name: CRA, NIS2 and NIST SSDF crosswalk
description: Each requirement of the Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) Annex I and Articles 13(5) and 14, mapped to the NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 provisions and NIST SSDF 1.1 practices that ask for the same or a related outcome.
status: Editorial judgement by Porta Regulus B.V. No authoritative crosswalk between these three instruments exists. Meeting one instrument does not meet another: the CRA regulates products, NIS2 Article 21 regulates an entity's own systems, and SSDF is voluntary guidance.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-218 Rev. 1, initial public draft

relations.direct: The other instrument asks for the same outcome.
relations.partial: The other instrument asks for part of the outcome, or for a wider outcome that includes it.
relations.none: No counterpart in the other instrument.

legalLinks.summary: The CRA aims to facilitate the compliance of digital infrastructure providers with the NIS2 supply chain requirements.
The CRA will facilitate compliance with the supply chain security obligations of entities in the scope of NIS2 and DORA.
The CRA takes its definitions of incident, near miss and CSIRT designated as coordinator from NIS2.

citation: CVD Portal, "CRA, NIS2 and NIST SSDF crosswalk", 2026-10-17. https://cradata.eu/crosswalk (CC BY 4.0)

ssdf.label: Define Security Requirements for Software Development
Communicate requirements to all third parties who will provide commercial software components to the organization for reuse by the organization’s own software.
Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity
Collect, safeguard, maintain, and share provenance data for all components of each software release (e.g., in a software bill of materials [SBOM]).
Design Software to Meet Security Requirements and Mitigate Security Risks
Review the Software Design to Verify Compliance with Security Requirements and Risk Information
Verify that acquired commercial, open-source, and all other third-party software components comply with the requirements, as defined by the organization, throughout their life cycles.
Configure the Compilation, Interpreter, and Build Processes to Improve Executable Security
Review and/or Analyze Human-Readable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements
Test Executable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements
Configure Software to Have Secure Settings by Default
Identify and Confirm Vulnerabilities on an Ongoing Basis

Gather information from software acquirers, users, and public sources on potential vulnerabilities in the software and third-party components that the software uses, and investigate all credible reports.
Have a policy that addresses vulnerability disclosure and remediation, and implement the roles, responsibilities, and processes needed to support that policy.
Analyze Vulnerabilities to Identify Their Root Causes

cra.label: Appropriate level of cybersecurity based on the risks

rows.basis: All three start from a risk assessment. NIS2 applies it to the entity's own systems and SSDF to the development process, so neither covers the product outcome the CRA requires.
SSDF finds vulnerabilities in own and third-party code before release and remediates them, which is the activity that lets a product ship without known exploitable vulnerabilities.
PW.9 asks for secure settings by default, the same outcome. NIS2 covers secure configuration only as part of development and maintenance.

SSDF 1.1 requires remediation but not a delivery channel, and the 1.2 draft adds PS.4 for robust updates. The CRA adds automatic updates by default, user notification and postponement, which neither other instrument asks for.
NIS2 asks for access control and multi-factor authentication on the entity's own systems. SSDF reaches it only through security requirements and design.
NIS2 asks for a cryptography policy for the entity. SSDF reaches confidentiality only through security requirements and design.
PS.2 protects the integrity of the release, which covers programs but not stored data or configuration at run time.
Data minimisation is a data protection principle. Neither NIS2 Article 21 nor SSDF asks for it.
NIS2 business continuity covers the entity's services, not the product's essential functions. SSDF reaches availability only through design.
The impact of a product on other networks has no NIS2 counterpart. SSDF reaches it only through design.
Attack surface reduction is a design decision. SSDF asks for the design and its review, not for the outcome.
PW.6 configures the build to improve executable security, which is where most exploitation mitigation techniques are switched on.
NIS2 incident handling needs detection on the entity's own systems. SSDF has no practice for logging in the delivered product.
Secure removal of user data and settings has no counterpart in NIS2 Article 21 or SSDF.
PS.3.2 asks for provenance data for every component of a release, such as an SBOM. NIS2 needs the same inventory for supply chain security and asset management.
All three ask for vulnerabilities to be assessed and remediated. The CRA adds that security updates ship separately from functionality updates where feasible.
SSDF code review and testing are the regular tests and reviews the CRA names. NIS2 asks for effectiveness to be assessed, which testing evidences.
Public advisories for fixed vulnerabilities follow from a disclosure policy. Only the CRA sets their content and the condition that an update is available first.
NIS2 names vulnerability disclosure in 21(2)(e) and RV.1.3 asks for a disclosure policy. The CRA adds that the policy is enforced.
RV.1.1 gathers reports from users and researchers, which needs the contact address the CRA requires. NIS2 21(3) covers supplier vulnerabilities from the receiving side.
PS.2 lets a recipient verify a release, and the 1.2 draft adds PS.4 for robust updates. The CRA asks for the whole distribution mechanism, automatic where applicable.
SSDF requires remediation. Free of charge and advisory messages are CRA-only conditions.
All three ask the receiving party to check the security of what it takes from suppliers. The CRA applies it to components integrated in the product, NIS2 to the entity's suppliers.

Both use a 24-hour early warning and a 72-hour notification. The CRA trigger is an actively exploited vulnerability in a product and the NIS2 trigger is a significant incident at the entity. The CRA final report is due 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available, the NIS2 final report one month after the notification. SSDF has no reporting to authorities.

Same 24-hour, 72-hour and one-month structure as NIS2. The recipients differ: a CRA report goes through the ENISA single reporting platform to the CSIRT designated as coordinator, a NIS2 report to the national CSIRT or competent authority. No provision makes one report count as the other.
